"Nothing Compares 2 U" was written by the American musician [[Prince (musician)|Prince]], who recorded a demo in 1984. In 1985, Prince's [[funk]] band [[The Family (band)|the Family]] released its sole studio album, ''[[The Family (The Family album)|The Family]],'' including "Nothing Compares 2 U". It was not released as a single and received little recognition. Prince's demo was released in 2018.<ref name="Pitchfork">{{cite web|title=Listen to Prince's Original Version of "Nothing Compares 2 U"|url=https://pitchfork.com/news/listen-to-princes-original-version-of-nothing-compares-2-u|work=[[Pitchfork (website)|Pitchfork]]|date=April 19, 2018|access-date=April 26, 2018|language=en}}</ref>

In 1993, Prince released a live version of "Nothing Compares 2 U", with [[Rosie Gaines]] on guest vocals, on his compilation album ''[[The Hits/The B-Sides]]''. His 1984 demo was released as a single in 2018 and included on the 2019 compilation ''[[Originals (Prince album)|Originals]]''.

Prince's 1984 demo, remixed by [[Tony Maserati]], was released as a single in 2018, and later on the posthumous compilation [[Originals (Prince album)|''Originals'']], by [[Warner Bros. "Nothing Compares 2 U" was written by the American musician Prince, who recorded a demo in 1984. In 1985, Prince's funk band the Family released its sole studio album, The Family, including "Nothing Compares 2 U". It was not released as a single and received little recognition. Prince's demo was released in 2018.

In 1993, Prince released a live version of "Nothing Compares 2 U", with Rosie Gaines on guest vocals, on his compilation album The Hits/The B-Sides. His 1984 demo was released as a single in 2018 and included on the 2019 compilation Originals.

Prince's 1984 demo, remixed by Tony Maserati, was released as a single in 2018, and later on the posthumous compilation Originals, by Warner Bros. Records in conjunction with his estate. It was accompanied by a music video, consisting of edited rehearsal footage shot in mid-1984. The single reached number 21 on the US Hot R&B Songs chart and number eight on the US R&B Digital Song Sales chart in 2018. This version also reached number seven on the US Bubbling Under Hot 100 chart in 1993. Following Prince's death in 2016, this version reached number 43 on the US Digital Songs Sales chart and number 31 on the US R&B/Hip-Hop Digital Song Sales chart.

sections.heading: Recording
sections.wikitext:
[[Sinéad O'Connor]] recorded "Nothing Compares 2 U" with a new arrangement by her and the producer [[Nellee Hooper]]. O'Connor's version is in the [[Key (music)|key]] of [[F major]].<ref>{{Cite web|last1=Prince|last2=Sinead|first2=O'Connor|date=August 2, 2010|title=Nothing Compares 2 U|url=https://www.musicnotes.com/sheetmusic/mtd.asp?ppn=MN0082563|access-date=April 28, 2021|website=Musicnotes.com}}</ref>

Pre-production for the song was done at Hooper's house. Hooper enlisted [[Gota Yashiki]], with whom he'd previously worked on [[Soul II Soul]]'s [[Club Classics Vol. One|debut studio album]], to do arranging and programming of instrument and drum tracks for the song. Yashiki utilized an [[Atari ST]] computer running [[Logic Pro#Creator and Notator|C-Lab Notator]] [[Music sequencer#software sequencer|sequencing software]] and an [[Akai S1000|Akai S1100]] [[Sampler (musical instrument)|sampler]]. After recording sessions moved to [[Britannia Row Studios]], live drum parts were overdubbed and the cello part, provided by the Akai sampler, was finalized.<ref name=SOSFeb2012/> 

O'Connor's vocals were recorded in a single [[take]], then [[double-tracked]] with another subsequent take, using an [[AKG (company)|AKG]] C414B-ULS large-diaphragm [[condenser microphone]]. Per the singer's demands, absolutely no [[Dynamic range compression|compression]] was to be used on her vocals.<ref name=SOSFeb2012/>

Sinéad O'Connor recorded "Nothing Compares 2 U" with a new arrangement by her and the producer Nellee Hooper. O'Connor's version is in the key of F major.

Pre-production for the song was done at Hooper's house. Hooper enlisted Gota Yashiki, with whom he'd previously worked on Soul II Soul's debut studio album, to do arranging and programming of instrument and drum tracks for the song. Yashiki utilized an Atari ST computer running C-Lab Notator sequencing software and an Akai S1100 sampler. After recording sessions moved to Britannia Row Studios, live drum parts were overdubbed and the cello part, provided by the Akai sampler, was finalized. 

O'Connor's vocals were recorded in a single take, then double-tracked with another subsequent take, using an AKG C414B-ULS large-diaphragm condenser microphone. Per the singer's demands, absolutely no compression was to be used on her vocals.

sections.heading: Critical reception
sections.wikitext:
{{Quote box
| width = 30%
| align = right
| quote = "A few times each year a song comes along that deserves extra-special recognition. Here's the first such entry of 1990. Since I've been shouting the praises of Sinéad's remarkable interpretation of this [[Prince (musician)|Prince]]-penned tune to many of you for over a month, it was safe to assume it would eventually end up on this page. Absolutely brilliant—and if you haven't caught the video, do yourself a favor and check it out NOW!"
| source = —Dave Sholin from the ''[[Gavin Report]]'' talking about the song.<ref>{{cite magazine|first= Dave |last= Sholin |title= Gavin Picks > Singles |magazine= [[Gavin Report]] |issue= 1797 |date= March 9, 1990 |page= 52 |access-date= April 17, 2018 |url= https://www.worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Gavin-Report/90/90/Gavin-1990-03-09.pdf}}</ref>
}}
O'Connor's version received mostly positive reviews. Jodi Cleesattle from ''American Eagle'' felt that "there is pain in Sinéad O'Connor's voice, and there probably always will be". She remarked that "loneliness and longing" are highlighted on the song, adding that O'Connor's voice "fits the song perfectly. Her vocals soar and leap unexpectedly but gracefully, making, the [[Ballad (music)|ballad]], the loveliest of love songs."<ref>{{cite magazine|first= Jodi |last= Cleesattle |title= Pain, power essence of O'Connor's voice |magazine= American Eagle |date= April 2, 1990 |page= 15 }}</ref> Bill Coleman from ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'' magazine named it a "brilliant interpretation of the melancholic lament."<ref>{{cite magazine|first=Bill|last=Coleman|url=https://www.worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Billboard/90s/1990/BB-1990-03-10.pdf|title=Single Reviews|magazine=[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]|date=March 10, 1990|access-date=February 15, 2020|page=91}}</ref> Ernest Hardy from ''[[Cashbox (magazine)|Cashbox]]'' called it a "genuine tear-jerker".<ref>{{cite magazine|first= Ernest |last= Hardy |title= Pop Reviews: Albums |magazine= [[Cashbox (magazine)|Cashbox]] |date= March 31, 1990 |page= 18 |access-date= October 27, 2020 |url= https://worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Cash-Box/90s/1990/CB-1990-03-31.pdf}}</ref>

[[Greg Sandow]] for ''[[Entertainment Weekly]]'' felt it is a song "about how to carry on after losing love".<ref>{{cite magazine|first=Greg|last=Sandow|url=https://ew.com/article/1990/03/16/i-do-not-want-what-i-havent-got/|title=I Do not Want What I Haven't Got|magazine=[[Entertainment Weekly]]|date=March 16, 1990|access-date=February 23, 2020|author-link=Greg Sandow}}</ref> Tom Moon from ''[[Knight Ridder]]'' said she "adapts the breathy approach of a torch singer."<ref>{{cite magazine|first=Tom|last=Moon|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Z-4iAAAAIBAJ|title=Sinead O'Connor produces a stunning second album|magazine=[[Spokane Chronicle]]|date=March 23, 1990|access-date=March 13, 2020}}</ref> A reviewer from ''[[Los Angeles Times]]'' noted that the singer "match raw emotion with spare sounds" on "the quiet, desperate, lovelorn beauty".<ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1990-03-18-ca-757-story.html|title=Sinead O'Connor "I Do Not Want What I Haven't Got"|magazine=[[Los Angeles Times]]|date=March 18, 1990|access-date=February 26, 2020}}</ref> ''[[Melody Maker]]'' wrote, "It should go without saying that her voice is brilliant, but this is a pointless and embarrassing over-sentimental paw. The zillions of strings don't help, they don't add poignancy, they merely serve to drag the momentum backwards. [...] A waste of talent."<ref>{{cite magazine|author=Push|magazine=[[Melody Maker]]|title=Singles|url=https://www.flickr.com/photos/nothingelseon/52014187340/|date=January 6, 1990|access-date=February 24, 2023}}</ref>

[[Pan-European identity|Pan-European]] magazine ''[[Music & Media]]'' stated that out of all the recent covers of Prince songs – [[Chaka Khan]]'s "[[I Feel for You]]", [[Tom Jones (singer)|Tom Jones]]' "[[Kiss (Prince song)#The Art of Noise featuring Tom Jones version|Kiss]]" and [[Simple Minds]]' "[[Sign o' the Times (song)|Sign o' the Times]]" – "this is definitely the most convincing." The reviewer noted further that originally recorded by [[Minneapolis]] band the Family for their 1985 debut album, "O'Connor's emotionally charged version has immediate appeal", and is "destined to be her biggest hit to date."<ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://worldradiohistory.com/UK/Music-and-Media/90s/1990/MM-1990-02-03.pdf|title=Previews: Singles|magazine=[[Music & Media]]|date=February 3, 1990|page=16|access-date=February 19, 2020}}</ref> David Giles from ''[[Music Week]]'' found that the song "is not one of Prince's finest moments, and O'Connor does little to disguise this fact bar a few token vocal [[somersault]]s. The string [[Synthesizer|synths]] also have a dirge-like effect, dragging the rest of the arrangement along with them."<ref>{{cite magazine|first= David |last= Giles |title= Singles |magazine= [[Music Week]] |date= January 13, 1990 |access-date= October 29, 2020 |url= https://worldradiohistory.com/UK/Music-Week/1990/MW-1990-01-13.pdf}}</ref>

''The Network Forty''{{'}}s reviewer wrote that "when Sinéad sang 'Nothing Compares 2 U', seas calmed, angels wept and [[Top 40]] radio stood still to listen to this powerful expression of unrequited love."<ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://www.worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Archive-Network-40/90/Network-40-1990-12-21.pdf|title=Musical Memories of 1990|magazine=The Network Forty|date=December 21, 1990|page=6|access-date=March 21, 2020}}</ref> James Brown  from ''[[New Musical Express|NME]]'' said, "Pining for a recently departed love, Sinéad hits the lyrics with an immense range of vocal ability and passion. From a gossamer thin whisper to a searing plea she shows just how much catching up [[Kate Bush]] has to do."<ref>{{cite magazine|first=James|last=Brown|magazine=[[New Musical Express|NME]]|title=Singles|url=https://www.flickr.com/photos/nothingelseon/52027358238/|date=January 20, 1990|access-date=February 24, 2023}}</ref> Tom Doyle from ''[[Smash Hits]]'' felt that "it doesn't sound at all like any of her other stuff."<ref>{{cite magazine|first=Tom|last=Doyle|url=https://www.flickr.com/photos/smashhits90s/35546288695/in/album-72157682695959053/|title=Review: LPs|magazine=[[Smash Hits]]|issue=294|page=55|date=March 7, 1990|access-date=March 8, 2020}}</ref>

sections.heading: Commercial performance
sections.wikitext:
O'Connor's version was a worldwide hit, topping charts in O'Connor's native Ireland, Australia, Austria, Canada, Denmark, Germany, Mexico, Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, Sweden, Switzerland, the United Kingdom and the United States (plus top five in France). It was certified platinum in Austria and in the United Kingdom, and gold in Germany and in Sweden.

In the United States it spent four weeks at the top of the [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]]; in addition, it was number one on the [[Alternative Songs|''Billboard'' Alternative Songs]] chart and reached number two on the [[Billboard Adult Contemporary|''Billboard'' Adult Contemporary]] chart (held off the top position by [[Rod Stewart]]'s "[[This Old Heart of Mine (Is Weak for You)#Rod Stewart versions|This Old Heart of Mine]]" for three weeks). In terms of its chart performance on the Hot 100 it ranked number three for 1990. In April 1990, it was certified [[Music recording sales certification|platinum]] by the [[Recording Industry Association of America]]. On the second of its four weeks at number one, the record's parent album ''I Do Not Want What I Haven't Got'' started a six-week run at number one on the [[Billboard 200|''Billboard'' 200]]. In 2019, the single ranked 97 in a Hot 100 60th-anniversary Top 600 covering the period from 1958 to 2018.

In the United Kingdom the single ranked [[1990 in British music#Best-selling singles of 1990|number two for the year]], behind a re-release of [[the Righteous Brothers]]' "[[Unchained Melody#The Righteous Brothers versions|Unchained Melody]]".<ref>{{Cite magazine |date=January 5, 1991 |title=Best selling albums & singles of 1990 |url=https://www.flickr.com/photos/nothingelseon/52265646176/in/album-72177720301080070/ |magazine=[[Melody Maker]] |page=2 |volume=67 |issue=1}}</ref> In July 2023, days [[Sinéad O'Connor#Death|after O'Connor's death]], "Nothing Compares 2 U" reappeared on the UK Top 100 at number 45,<ref>{{cite web |date=July 28, 2023 |title=Official Singles Chart Top 100 28 July 2023 - 3 August 2023 |url=https://www.officialcharts.com/charts/singles-chart/ |access-date=July 28, 2023 |website=Official Charts}}</ref> and charted at number 1 on the UK Singles Downloads Chart.<ref>{{cite web |date=July 28, 2023 |title=Official Singles Downloads Chart on 28/7/2023 28 July 2023 - 3 August 2023 |url=https://www.officialcharts.com/charts/singles-downloads-chart/20230728/7000/ |access-date=July 28, 2023 |website=Official Charts}}</ref>

O'Connor's version was a worldwide hit, topping charts in O'Connor's native Ireland, Australia, Austria, Canada, Denmark, Germany, Mexico, Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, Sweden, Switzerland, the United Kingdom and the United States (plus top five in France). It was certified platinum in Austria and in the United Kingdom, and gold in Germany and in Sweden.

In the United States it spent four weeks at the top of the Billboard Hot 100; in addition, it was number one on the Billboard Alternative Songs chart and reached number two on the Billboard Adult Contemporary chart (held off the top position by Rod Stewart's "This Old Heart of Mine" for three weeks). In terms of its chart performance on the Hot 100 it ranked number three for 1990. In April 1990, it was certified platinum by the Recording Industry Association of America. On the second of its four weeks at number one, the record's parent album I Do Not Want What I Haven't Got started a six-week run at number one on the Billboard 200. In 2019, the single ranked 97 in a Hot 100 60th-anniversary Top 600 covering the period from 1958 to 2018.

In the United Kingdom the single ranked number two for the year, behind a re-release of the Righteous Brothers' "Unchained Melody". In July 2023, days after O'Connor's death, "Nothing Compares 2 U" reappeared on the UK Top 100 at number 45, and charted at number 1 on the UK Singles Downloads Chart.

[[File:NothingCompares2U.PNG|thumb|right|The lone face of O'Connor made the video one of the most recognizable of the 1990s.]]Directed by John Maybury, the music video consists mostly of a close-up of O'Connor's face as she goes through stages of sadness and anger while singing the lyrics; the rest consists of her walking through the [[Parc de Saint-Cloud]] in Paris. Toward the end of the video, two tears roll down her face, one on each cheek. O'Connor has said that her tears were real. She did not intend to cry but then thought, "I should let this happen."<ref name="songfacts.com">{{cite web |title=Nothing Compares 2 U by Sinéad O'Connor Songfacts |url=http://www.songfacts.com/detail.php?id=642 |website=Songfacts.com}}</ref> She explained that the tears were triggered by thoughts of her mother, who died in a car accident in 1985.<ref name="songfacts.com" /> She said she learned to channel her emotions with the "[[bel canto]]" singing style, which she compared to [[Method acting#Misconceptions|extreme acting methods]].<ref>{{cite web |last=Laurence |first=Rebecca |title=Prince's heartbreaking song about loss |date=April 22, 2016 |url=http://www.bbc.com/culture/story/20160422-princes-heartbreaking-song-about-loss}}</ref> In the middle and at the very end of the video, there is a shot from O'Connor's photo session for the ''I Do Not Want What I Haven't Got'' album cover.

The video received its world premiere on MTV's late-night alternative rock program ''[[120 Minutes]]'' on January 28, 1990.<ref>{{cite web|title=Sinead O'Connor 120 Minutes X-Ray|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=J95UEfYxW8I&t=23s&ab_channel=MarkPakula|website=YouTube|access-date=April 18, 2025|date=January 28, 1990}}</ref> It won three "[[MTV Video Music Awards|Moonmen]]" at the [[1990 MTV Video Music Awards]]: [[MTV Video Music Award for Video of the Year|Video of the Year]] (O'Connor was the first female artist to be awarded it), [[MTV Video Music Award for Best Female Video|Best Female Video]] and [[MTV Video Music Award for Best Post-Modern Video|Best Post-Modern Video]]. It was nominated for [[MTV Video Music Award – Breakthrough Video|Breakthrough Video]], [[MTV Video Music Award – Viewer's Choice|Viewer's Choice]] and [[MTV Video Music Award for International Viewer's Choice|International Viewer's Choice]] during the ceremony. The video was also the subject of many parodies and spoofs, such as [[Gina Riley]]'s parody "Nothing Is There" on ''[[Fast Forward (Australian TV series)|Fast Forward]],'' referring to the fact that O'Connor tended to shave her head bald.<ref>{{cite web |date=April 21, 2009 |title=Gina Riley - Nothing is There!!! From Fast Forward |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8jYPrZ2PA88 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211117/8jYPrZ2PA88 |archive-date=November 17, 2021 |access-date=September 1, 2016 |publisher=YouTube}}{{cbignore}}</ref>

sections.wikitext:
In 2019, Bill Lamb from [[About.com]] wrote that O'Connor's "emotional, gutsy performance made it a classic. Painful loss meets stunning vocal beauty with a perfectly understated instrumental arrangement."<ref>{{cite web |last=Lamb |first=Bill |date=September 7, 2019 |title=The Best 100 Songs From the 1990s |url=https://www.liveabout.com/top-songs-from-the-90s-3245307 |access-date=March 21, 2020 |publisher=[[About.com]] |archive-date=May 17, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210517170314/https://www.liveabout.com/top-songs-from-the-90s-3245307 |url-status=dead }}</ref> In their 2020 retrospective review, Matthew Hocter from ''Albumism'' described it as a song "deeply rooted in emotion and despair which would go on to certify O'Connor and that song as one of music history's most unforgettable moments."<ref>{{cite web |date=March 18, 2020 |title=Sinéad O'Connor's 'I Do Not Want What I Haven't Got' Turns 30: Anniversary Retrospective |url=https://www.albumism.com/features/sinead-oconnor-i-do-not-want-what-i-havent-got-turns-30-anniversary-retrospective |access-date=March 23, 2020 |publisher=Albumism}}</ref> [[AllMusic]] editor Steve Huey called the song "stunning" and noted its "remarkable intimacy".<ref>{{cite web |last=Huey |first=Steve |title=Sinéad O'Connor - I Do Not Want What I Haven't Got |url=https://www.allmusic.com/album/i-do-not-want-what-i-havent-got-mw0000654778 |access-date=March 21, 2020 |publisher=[[AllMusic]]}}</ref>

In 2010, Tom Ewing of ''[[Freaky Trigger]]'' noted it as a "very moving track", and added that it "captures the stasis, anger and devastation of a bad break-up with awful accuracy." He also complimented the music "whose stately, sympathetic pulse gives O'Connor the canvas she needs to be so devastating."<ref>{{cite web |last=Ewing |first=Tom |date=October 29, 2010 |title=Sinead O'Connor – "Nothing Compares 2 U" |url=http://freakytrigger.co.uk/ft/2010/10/sinead-oconnor-nothing-compares-2-u/#more-20020 |access-date=March 6, 2020 |publisher=[[Freaky Trigger]]}}</ref> In a 2000 review, Steven Wells from ''[[NME]]'' said "it remains one of the best 'boo-hoo, my bloke's left me' pop songs ever recorded", and a "stark reminder that O'Connor is blessed with an amazing and unique voice". He concluded with that it "remains the outstanding highlight of her career to date. She's more than capable of surpassing it in the future. Less [[Sade (singer)|Sade]] and more [[Aretha Franklin|Aretha]], please."<ref>{{cite web |last=Wells |first=Steven |title=Sinead O'Connor – So Far... The Best Of... Sinead O'Connor |url=http://www.nme.com/reviews/reviews/19980101000788reviews.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20000817172905/http://www.nme.com/reviews/reviews/19980101000788reviews.html |archive-date=August 17, 2000 |access-date=December 4, 2020 |work=[[NME]]}}</ref>

In 2009, Mark Richardson from ''[[Pitchfork (website)|Pitchfork]]'' stated that "you have to look pretty hard to find a better expression in [[pop music]] of the void that exists when a relationship ends."<ref>{{cite web |last=Richardson |first=Mark |date=April 24, 2009 |title=Sinéad O'Connor: I Do Not Want What I Haven't Got (Limited Edition) |url=http://pitchfork.com/reviews/albums/12954-i-do-not-want-what-i-havent-got-limted-edition/ |access-date=March 7, 2020 |work=[[Pitchfork (website)|Pitchfork]]}}</ref> In a 2015 retrospective review, ''Pop Rescue'' wrote that O'Connor "makes light work" of the track, and she's "having plenty of power to belt out the lyrics at the right points." The reviewer added that it is a "fantastic exhibit of [[1990s in music|90s music]]".<ref>{{cite web |date=October 5, 2015 |title=Review: "I Do Not Want What I Haven't Got" by Sinead O'Connor (CD, 1990) |url=https://poprescue.com/2015/10/05/pop-rescue-i-do-not-want-what-i-havent-got-by-sinead-oconnor-cd-1990/ |access-date=April 14, 2020 |publisher=Pop Rescue}}</ref> In 2004, Sal Cinquemani from ''[[Slant Magazine]]'' felt that it perhaps is O'Connor's "greatest vocal achievement" and described it as a "classic torch song she quite simply owns."<ref>{{cite magazine |last=Cinquemani |first=Sal |title=I Do Not Want What I Haven't Got |url=http://www.slantmagazine.com/music/music_review.asp?ID=347 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070930153643/http://www.slantmagazine.com/music/music_review.asp?ID=347 |archive-date=September 30, 2007 |access-date=February 26, 2020 |magazine=[[Slant Magazine]]}}</ref>

AllMusic editor Steve Huey called the song "stunning" and noted its "remarkable intimacy".

He concluded with that it "remains the outstanding highlight of her career to date. She's more than capable of surpassing it in the future. Less Sade and more Aretha, please."

* An orchestral version of the song was featured on [[Dune (band)|Dune]]'s 1997 album [[Forever (Dune_album)|Forever]].
* In 2006, Scottish singer-songwriter [[King Creosote]] released a cover version of the song.
* In 2014, [[Aretha Franklin]] released her 38th and final studio album ''[[Aretha Franklin Sings the Great Diva Classics]]'' in which she covered several songs by other female recording artists, including an upbeat, [[jazz]] version of "Nothing Compares 2 U".
* On May 4, 2016, the song was simulcast on radio stations throughout the United States to commemorate Prince 15 days after his death. The simulcast was timed to reflect the song's opening lyric: "It's been 7 hours and 15 days since you took your love away."<ref>{{cite news |last=Trust |first=Gary |date=May 3, 2016 |title=Billboard |url=https://www.billboard.com/articles/news/7356754/prince-nothing-compares-2-u-radio-simulcast |access-date=April 19, 2018}}</ref>
* [[Chris Cornell]] posted a link to his version the day after Prince's death. In an accompanying message, he wrote: "Prince's music is the soundtrack to the soulful and beautiful universe he created, and we have all been privileged to be part of that amazing world. I performed his song 'Nothing Compares 2 U' for the first time a couple months ago. It has a timeless relevance for me and practically everyone I know. Sadly, now his own lyrics in this song could not be more relevant than at this moment, and I sing them now in reverence as I pay tribute to this unequaled artist who has given all of our lives so much inspiration and made the world so much more interesting. We will miss you Prince!!!"<ref>{{cite web |date=April 22, 2016 |title=CHRIS CORNELL: 'PRINCE's Music Is The Soundtrack To The Soulful And Beautiful Universe He Created' |url=http://www.blabbermouth.net/news/chris-cornell-princes-music-is-the-soundtrack-to-the-soulful-and-beautiful-universe-he-created/ |website=Blabbermouth}}</ref> On [[Father's Day]] 2018, Cornell's daughter Toni released a version of the song she recorded with her father before his death in 2017.<ref>{{cite web |date=June 17, 2018 |title=Chris Cornell and his daughter cover Prince's 'Nothing Compares 2 U': Stream |url=https://consequence.net/2018/06/chris-cornell-daughter-prince/ |website=Consequence}}</ref> In 2020, the song was covered on Chris Cornell's ''[[No One Sings Like You Anymore, Vol. 1]]''.<ref>{{cite web |last=Grow |first=Kory |date=December 11, 2020 |title=Chris Cornell's Historic Voice and Great Ear Take Center Stage on the Covers LP, 'No One Sings Like You Anymore' |url=https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-album-reviews/chris-cornell-no-one-sings-like-you-anymore-review-1101439/ |website=rollingstone.com}}</ref>
* In 2016, [[Madonna]] performed a rendition of this song alongside "[[Purple Rain (song)|Purple Rain]]" with [[Stevie Wonder]] at that year's [[2016 Billboard Music Awards|Billboard Music Awards]].
* [[Country music|Country]] artist [[Jon Pardi]] covered the song on his album ''Rancho Fiesta Sessions'' in 2020.
* In 2024, [[Annie Lennox]], accompanied by [[Wendy & Lisa]] sang this song at the [[66th Annual Grammy Awards|2024 Grammy Awards]] during the "In Memoriam" segment as a tribute to O'Connor. During the performance she had a tear painted on her cheek in homage to a similar scene in the song's music video.<ref>{{cite magazine |last1=Madarang |first1=Charisma |last2=Grow |first2=Kory |date=February 5, 2024 |title=Tony Bennett, Sinead O'Connor, Tina Turner Honored During In Memoriam at 2024 Grammys |url=https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/grammys-2024-in-memoriam-tribute-1234956928/ |access-date=February 5, 2024 |magazine=Rolling Stone}}</ref> She ended the performance by saying "Artists for ceasefire! Peace in the world!" as a response to the [[2023 Gaza war ceasefire]] and the [[Gaza war]]. The statement was also seen as a tribute to O'Connor's political outspokenness.<ref>{{cite magazine |last=Nichols |first=John |date=February 6, 2024 |title=And the Winner Is… Annie Lennox and Artists for Cease-Fire |url=https://www.thenation.com/article/activism/annie-lennox-grammys-ceasefire/ |access-date=February 15, 2024 |magazine=The National}}</ref>
* In 2025 at the [[Saturday Night Live 50th Anniversary Special]] the song was performed by [[Miley Cyrus]] and [[Brittany Howard]] with backing by [[The Roots]].<ref>{{Cite AV media |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sGrzWnT6NwY&feature=youtu.be |title=Miley Cyrus with Brittany Howard and The Roots: Nothing Compares 2 U (Live) – SNL50 |date=February 16, 2025 |last=Night Live |access-date=February 17, 2025 |via=YouTube}}</ref>
